   indicators, the known pitfalls and the questions to ask, each with its source. Interpretation without them is

   anisotropic crystals).

- One spectrum rarely fixes layer number alone; name the observable and its threshold.

7	## Calibration and spectral accuracy
8	- A first-order (linear) pixel-to-wavelength calibration of a single-grating spectrograph gave Raman shift
9	  errors of 5.0 to -6.8 cm-1 across the detector; with only 3 Hg lines, up to 18 cm-1; adding the quadratic
10	  term brought it within +-0.3 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024; arXiv 1209.0234, Methods p.10).
11	  Their check: graphite G 1581.5 +- 0.3 cm-1 over 12 spots.
12	- The error depends on where on the detector a line falls, so a single Si-line check near 520 cm-1 does not
13	  validate a 2D band near 2700 cm-1 [inference from the same mechanism].
14	- Si first order is quoted as 520 (Lee et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695; arXiv 1005.2509) and 520.9 cm-1
15	  (Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014, arXiv 1403.0499, p.7) in different setups: small offsets between labs are
16	  normal, so compare shifts relative to an internal reference measured in the same session.
17	
18	## Resolution, grating and instrument line shape
19	- Measure resolution from the Rayleigh line: 1.9 vs 9.4 cm-1 on two instruments in one study; spectra then fit
20	  with Voigt profiles and the Lorentzian FWHM taken as the lifetime width (Das et al. 2008, Nat. Nanotechnol.
21	  3, 210; arXiv 0709.1174, p.2). About 0.6 cm-1 with a triple-filter low-frequency setup (Zhang et al. 2013,
22	  PRB 87, 115413; arXiv 1212.6796, p.2); 2.7 cm-1 in Lee 2010 (docs/verified-reference-numbers.md).
23	- Widths near the resolution (hBN 3 to 9 cm-1, BP Ag2 3 to 7 cm-1; see material notes) are instrument-limited:
24	  never compare raw FWHM across setups without the resolution. A 0.5 cm-1 resolution was not enough to count BP
25	  layers from positions (Castellanos-Gomez 2014, p.8).
26	
27	## Laser heating, power density and photodamage
28	- Do a power series: Ferrari et al. 2006 saw no change from about 4 to 0.04 mW at 100x (arXiv
29	  cond-mat/0606284, p.2); typical working powers 1 mW with about 1 um spot (Cancado et al. 2011, arXiv
30	  1105.0175, p.2), 0.23 mW (Zhang 2013, p.2), below 300 uW at 0.5 NA (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358,
31	  p.7). Quote power density, not power: the same mW gives different heating at different NA.
32	- Temperature coefficients depend on support: graphene 2D -0.034 cm-1/K supported vs -0.072 suspended
33	  (Calizo 2007, arXiv 0708.1223, Table I; Chen et al. via Lee et al. 2011, arXiv 1103.3337, p.2). Do not
34	  convert a shift into a temperature with a coefficient from a different geometry.
35	- Optothermal estimates need a peak-vs-T calibration, the absorbed (not incident) power, and a measured spot
36	  size; using two spot sizes helps (Malekpour and Balandin 2018, J. Raman Spectrosc. 49, 106; arXiv
37	  1710.09749, pp.4, 18).
38	- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry fails under resonance when incident and scattered windows differ (Ferrari
39	  and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12).
40	- Photodamage is dose-dependent: BP oxidation rate scales with fluence (Favron et al. 2015, arXiv 1408.0345,
41	  p.7); MnPS3 degraded at about 50 uW when one spot was illuminated 500 s or longer (Lim et al. 2021, Curr.
42	  Appl. Phys. 21, 1; doi 10.1016/j.cap.2020.09.017, pp.6-7, via Lit-RAG). Irreversible change in a repeat
43	  spectrum means damage, reversible shift means heating.
44	
45	## Objective NA, focus and polarization
46	- A tightly focused beam has longitudinal (out-of-plane) field components that can excite modes forbidden for
47	  purely in-plane fields (Grosche et al. 2020, Opt. Express, doi 10.1364/OE.388943; arXiv 1905.12325,
48	  abstract). How large this leakage is for a standard 100x/0.9 objective was not quantified in what I read.
49	  [magnitude not verified]
50	- In birefringent crystals the classical Raman tensor fails because polarization changes with depth; an
51	  effective tensor is needed (Kranert et al. 2016, PRL 116, 127401, abstract). In thin anisotropic flakes on
52	  SiO2/Si, anisotropic interference changes polar patterns with thickness (Kim et al. 2015, arXiv 1510.03263).
53	- Si substrate intensity depends on Si crystal orientation to the laser polarization (Castellanos-Gomez 2014,
54	  p.8): sample/Si intensity ratios need fixed sample rotation.
55	- Ask whether the analyzer is fixed and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization, or the sample rotates;
56	  grating efficiency is polarization dependent [practice].
57	
58	## Interference on SiO2/Si
59	- Graphene I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80,
60	  125422; arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Intensity ratios between bands at different shifts are
61	  stack-dependent.
62	- For MoS2 the sample intensity oscillates with thickness (interference maxima), but the ratio of sample to Si
63	  intensity becomes monotonic and gives thickness (Li et al. 2012, ACS Nano 6, 7381; arXiv 1308.3835,
64	  abstract, Fig. 4). Interference also changes optical contrast (Gorbachev et al. 2011, arXiv 1008.2868).
65	
66	## Encapsulation and overlayers
67	- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and changes doping (Neumann et
68	  al. 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, p.2); it narrows BP lines and reveals a surface mode (Urban et al., arXiv
69	  1711.08294, abstract). Compare encapsulated with encapsulated only.
70	- Overlayer lines can overlap sample lines: hBN E2g near 1366 cm-1 on graphene D (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat.
71	  Commun. 9, 5387, p.6, via Lit-RAG). Measure an overlayer-only reference spot.
72	
73	## Low-frequency modes and filters
74	- Shear and breathing modes (tens of cm-1) need notch or Bragg filters reaching about 5 to 10 cm-1 and
75	  plasma-line cleanup (Zhang 2013, p.2). Many production spectrometers cut above the graphene C mode, so absence
76	  below the cutoff is not evidence (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.2). Odd and even layer numbers scale differently
77	  (Zhang 2013, abstract).
78	
79	## Spikes, plasma lines, fluorescence, baseline
80	- Spikes and plasma lines: see ../artifacts.md (sources listed there, not re-verified here).
81	- Fluorescence or PL backgrounds: fit a local background with the peaks for broad bands; a global baseline can
82	  remove real broad signal [practice; see ../artifacts.md].
83	
84	## Fitting line shapes and over-fitting
85	- Report whether ratios use heights or areas: graphene defect relations use heights (Cancado 2011) and heights
86	  and areas diverge in stage 2 (Eckmann et al. 2012, arXiv 1207.2058, p.5).
87	- Number of components needs physics: 1L graphene 2D one, Bernal 2L four (Ferrari 2006, p.2); unresolved
88	  doublets (BP Ag2 in few layers, resolved only at 77 K, Favron 2015, p.10) appear as broadening. Adding peaks
89	  without a physical reason fits noise; compare models by an information criterion [practice].
90	- Fit overlapping neighbours jointly (WS2 2LA(M) and E2g, see ../artifacts.md; hBN and graphene D, Purdie 2018).
91	
92	## Comparing spectra from different setups
93	- Different lasers: dispersive bands (graphene D, 2D) move; resonances change relative intensities (Cancado
94	  2011; Kim et al. 2012, arXiv 1201.4221). Different spectrographs: calibration offsets of several cm-1 (Lee
95	  2012). Different substrates: interference changes ratios (Yoon 2009). Compare differences measured in one
96	  session, not absolute values across papers.
97	
98	## Mapping statistics
99	- A spectrum averages over the spot: sub-spot strain variations show up as width, not shift (Neumann 2015,
100	  Fig. 1); mono- and bilayers can vary strongly from sample to sample (Gorbachev 2011, p.4).
101	- Use many points and correlations: hundreds of map pixels per sample fell on a G-2D line of slope 2.2 (Lee
102	  2012, p.3, Fig. 2). Report distributions (histograms, median and spread), not one "representative" spectrum.
103	- Move the spot between acquisitions on sensitive materials (Lim 2021).
104	
105	## What to ask
106	- Laser line and power at sample, objective NA, spot size; grating, resolution, calibration lines and date.
107	- Substrate stack and oxide thickness; encapsulation; suspended or supported.
108	- Polarization geometry; temperature and atmosphere; exposure time; number of spectra and map size.
109	
110	## Reference figures
111	- Yoon 2009, arXiv 0908.4322, Fig. 2: G and 2D intensities and their ratio vs SiO2 thickness.
112	- Li 2012, arXiv 1308.3835, Fig. 4: MoS2/Si intensity ratios vs layer number, calculated and measured.
113	- Zhang 2013, arXiv 1212.6796, Fig. 4: shear and breathing positions vs layer number (odd vs even).
114	- Neumann 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, Fig. 1: maps and 2D-width histograms, hBN vs SiO2 support.

- Report whether ratios use heights or areas: graphene defect relations use heights (Cancado 2011) and heights

Its uncertainty (±0.3 cm-1 assumed) is my choice; the fit errors alone are smaller, but the line-shape model adds systematic error. The 1L-vs-2L difference is only 1.4 cm-1, so one measurement at one wavelength is weak evidence.

The 2LA(M)/E2g1 intensity ratio depends strongly on polarization (cross vs parallel) and on the substrate stack; I do not know the polarization or the SiO2 thickness, so the ratio is only supporting evidence.

structured_output.summary: Spot 1 is most likely a monolayer (1L), but this rests on one line-position relation at one laser wavelength and is not proven. Spot 2 is 3L or bulk-like; the same data cannot separate 3L from bulk. The key evidence is the A1g–E2g1 separation: 62.0 cm-1 at spot 1 (1L reference 62.0) and 64.7 cm-1 at spot 2 (3L 64.6, bulk 64.8). The A1g mode itself stiffens by about 2.8 cm-1 from spot 1 to spot 2 while E2g1 barely moves, which is the thickness trend in the literature. The two-peak fit matters: the single-peak fitters blend 2LA(M) with E2g1 and would have given a biased separation of 65.6 and 67.0 cm-1.

caveats: The layer assignment uses the separation Δ = ω(A1g) − ω(E2g1) from one CVD study at one laser wavelength (Berkdemir et al. 2013, 514.5 nm). Its uncertainty (±0.3 cm-1 assumed) is my choice; the fit errors alone are smaller, but the line-shape model adds systematic error. The 1L-vs-2L difference is only 1.4 cm-1, so one measurement at one wavelength is weak evidence.

The E2g1 / 2LA(M) doublet split is model-dependent. Reduced chi² is 162 (spot 1) and 220 (spot 2), so residual structure remains. A different line shape or baseline could move the E2g1 centre by a few tenths of a cm-1, and that moves Δ directly. The separation of the two fits (62.0 and 64.7) is the most reliable number here.

The 2LA(M)/E2g1 intensity ratio depends strongly on polarization (cross vs parallel) and on the substrate stack; I do not know the polarization or the SiO2 thickness, so the ratio is only supporting evidence.

Si/sample intensity ratio is qualitative. Spot 1 could be partly on an edge or a bare SiO2 region, which would also raise the Si signal. Without the oxide thickness and an interference model, the Si/sample ratio gives no quantitative thickness.

Peak positions are referenced to the Si line (520.79 to 520.91 cm-1, offset +0.09 to +0.21) and the A1g–E2g1 separation cancels most calibration error; the A1g shift of +2.8 cm-1 is far above the calibration scatter.
The 175.9 cm-1 band is labelled LA(M) by analogy with the 488 nm reference. It is not tabulated at 514.5 nm in the source, so the label is tentative.
questions_for_user: What were the laser power at the sample and the spot size? Power density affects heating, which can shift A1g and E2g1 by a few tenths of a cm-1, and it sets the photodamage risk.
Polarization geometry (parallel, crossed, or unpolarized)? The 2LA(M)/E2g1 intensity ratio depends strongly on it, and the cross-polarized E2g1 is the cleaner measurement.
What is the SiO2 thickness, and is it the same under both spots? The Si/sample intensity ratio and the optical contrast both depend on it.
Was spot 1 fully on the island, or near an edge? The strong Si line at spot 1 could be partly from bare SiO2 or from a thinner or edge region.

Is PL, AFM step height, or Raman mapping available to confirm the monolayer? A PL measurement would confirm 1L cheaply, and an AFM step height gives the thickness directly. Either would settle the 1L vs 2L question that the separation alone cannot close, and would also separate 3L from bulk for spot 2.

Is the 295 K measurement temperature the same as the reference temperature used in the separation relation? The relation values are from a source whose temperature is not stated in my notes, so I assumed room temperature matches.

Shear and breathing modes are below the 120 cm-1 data cutoff, so the low-frequency check for layer number is not available.
No interference-calibrated Si/sample curve was applied, so the thin-flake reading from the Si intensity is qualitative.

The 310 cm-1 band (Zhao 2013) was not checked quantitatively in the spot 1 residual; the spot 2 residual looked flat there.
